analysis.title: Why Has The US Economy Been So Resilient To Soaring Rates And Higher Oil Prices? Goldman Explains
key_insights: Goldman estimates US GDP grew 3.4% in Q3 2026 and forecasts 2.2% growth for 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis, close to its 2.3% potential growth estimate and 0.3pp below its start-of-year forecast.

Goldman says financial conditions have changed little on net since January: higher rates were nearly offset by higher equity prices, narrower credit spreads and a weaker dollar. The financial conditions impulse implies only a 0.1% hit to 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth.
Using the Fed's FRB/US model, Goldman finds higher rates hit residential investment meaningfully, offset by slight boosts to consumption and business investment.

Goldman's rule of thumb is that a sustained $10/barrel rise in oil lowers GDP growth by just over 0.1% through lower real purchasing power. Applied to this year's oil path, wider refined product spreads and its commodities forecasts, the drag is 0.4%.
A rise in the Q3 rig count index points to a pickup in energy capex. The consumption drag and capex boost net to a 0.3% hit to GDP growth from the oil shock, per Goldman.

Tighter financial conditions and higher oil together imply roughly a 0.4% GDP drag. Goldman's forecast downgrade is only slightly smaller than that, so the resilience puzzle is smaller than it appears.

Consumer spending explains the slight outperformance. Goldman's start-of-year forecast was 2.4% consumption growth for 2026 Q4/Q4. Its oil shock model implies a 0.6% hit, partly offset by a 0.2% equity wealth effect, for an expected 2.0%. Goldman now forecasts 2.2%, a 0.2% upside surprise, partly on solid recent data.

Morgan Stanley's Andrew Sheets notes US 10-year Treasury yields are up 100bp this year while global equities are up about 13%. Under the Gordon Growth model, valuation depends on the gap between required return (r) and growth (g), so equities can hold up if expected growth rises faster than rates.

UBS says investment outside technology has been in recession for at least two years. Private non-residential fixed investment averaged 0.1% YoY over 8 quarters (vs a 3.2% long-run average), residential averaged -2.0% (vs 2.2%), and AI-related investment grew 26% YoY. UBS concludes the scope for rates to depress spending further may be limited.

The author argues AI capex funded by new debt is the only driver of US growth. The article's closing view is that a stock selloff would remove the consumer wealth effect and most likely push the US into recession.

sector_views.rationale: Energy capex is picking up in Q3 as the rig count index rises, partly offsetting the oil price drag on consumption.
AI-related investment grew 26% YoY over eight quarters while non-tech investment was roughly flat, so tech capex is carrying US investment growth (UBS data cited in the article).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Growth is running above Goldman's 2.3% potential estimate, supported by consumer spending.
Close to potential growth and 0.3pp below the start-of-year forecast, a modest downgrade.
The 2026 forecast sits slightly below potential.
Consumption is the source of the outperformance against what the oil and market moves implied (2.0%).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Applied to this year's path the drag is 0.4% through consumption, and 0.3% net of the energy capex boost.

risk_factors: A stock market selloff would remove the equity wealth effect on consumption, and the article says the US would most likely slide into recession.
Growth depends on debt-funded AI capex. A bond market break or a failure of that funding would put the economy at risk.
Higher oil prices continue to erode real purchasing power, a 0.4% GDP drag in Goldman's estimate before the capex offset.
geopolitical: War with Iran has created uncertainty about the oil price outlook and initially held back US oil producers' capex.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman says financial conditions are little changed net, with higher yields offset by equities, tighter credit spreads and a weaker dollar. Rates and oil together are only about a 0.4% GDP drag, and consumption is growing 2.2%.
tension_points.bear_case: The article argues growth depends on debt-funded AI capex, non-tech investment has been in recession for two years, and a stock selloff would remove the wealth effect and likely cause a recession.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A stock market selloff that removes the equity wealth effect on consumption.
